---
title: The big picture
subtitle: What BDM is, in one sitting
aliases: [/explanations/index.html, /why/ecosystem.html]
---

BDM (Behaverse Data Model) is a specific, coherent, user-friendly, and interoperable way of organizing everything a behavioral study produces and consumes.

A cognitive science study draws on many kinds of information: behavioral data (key presses, choices), questionnaire responses, physiological signals, stimulus descriptions, instructions, task parameters, participant demographics, and much more. BDM aims to cover all of them, and for each one defines three things:

**What** it is
: The key concept a piece of information represents, and what it means. "Trial", for example, can refer to several distinct concepts, and "instructions" can be seen as a kind of stimulus. Pinning down the core data concepts of cognitive science is what makes it possible to organize the data consistently and meaningfully.

**How** it is encoded
: Which variables to record, what to call them, and the conventions their values follow. A controlled vocabulary ensures one concept is always named and encoded the same way—response time is always `response_time` in seconds, never `RT` or `reactionTime` in milliseconds.

**Where** it lives
: Where each kind of information is stored, and in what form—information about stimuli, for instance, goes in a stimulus table saved as a CSV file.

Because BDM specifies all of this exactly, a dataset can be validated, read by machines, and processed by automated pipelines—giving stronger quality control and transparency than the typical, per-study custom data-processing code.

BDM is not the only effort to improve how cognitive-science data is organized. Where it stands apart, in our view, is that it goes beyond describing metadata, naming files, and prescribing a folder layout: it tackles the harder problems of defining what the data itself should contain, how its variables are named and defined, and how the different kinds of information connect to each other. BDM prioritizes behavior because understanding behavior is essential to understanding the processes and computations that produce it, and the biology that supports it.

## The anatomy of a dataset

Perhaps the simplest way to see what BDM is, is to look at what a BDM dataset looks like. A BDM dataset is an ordinary folder, named after the study that produced it. Inside are subfolders holding data and metadata—organized as tidy tables or richer structured formats—whose columns and fields carry names and definitions drawn from a controlled vocabulary, and values and units that follow shared conventions.

```
my-study/
├─ README.md            # dataset card: what this is, who made it, license, etc.
├─ LICENSE
├─ instruments/         # the tasks and questionnaires used, with their parameters
│  ├─ stroop.yaml
│  └─ bisbas.yaml
├─ agents.csv           # who the data is about—one row per agent
└─ data/                # the data, partitioned by agent → session → activity
   └─ agent_001/
      ├─ studyflow.csv        # what this agent did, and in what order
      └─ session_1/
         ├─ stroop/           # a cognitive test
         │  ├─ events_1.ndjson    # events: what happened, as it happened
         │  ├─ response_1.csv     # trials: one row per trial
         │  ├─ stimulus_1.csv     # supporting table: the stimuli shown
         │  ├─ option_1.csv       # supporting table: the response options
         │  └─ input_1.csv        # supporting table: the raw inputs (key presses)
         └─ bisbas/           # a questionnaire—stored the same way
            ├─ response_1.csv
            ├─ stimulus_1.csv     # the questions
            └─ option_1.csv       # the answer options
```

Reading top to bottom:

- **`README.md`** is the [dataset card](/spec/dataset-cards.qmd): a human-readable description plus machine-readable metadata in its front matter—what the dataset is, who made it, its license, and a codebook defining every variable.
- **`LICENSE`** states the terms under which the data may be used.
- **`instruments/`** describes the tasks and questionnaires used to collect the data—one file per instrument, with its parameters.
- **`agents.csv`** lists who the data is about: one row per agent (a human participant or an artificial one), with their attributes.
- **`data/`** holds the data itself, partitioned by folders into `agent → session → activity`. Each agent's folder carries a **[`studyflow.csv`](/spec/studyflows.qmd)** recording which activities they completed and in what order, and one subfolder per session. Each session in turn holds one folder per activity—a cognitive test (`stroop/`) or a questionnaire (`bisbas/`); both are stored the same way.

Inside an activity folder, the raw **events** (`events_1.ndjson`) record what happened as it happened, and the **[Response table](/spec/trial/01-response.qmd)** (`response_1.csv`) holds the *trials* derived from those events—one row per trial. Supporting tables alongside it describe the stimuli shown (`stimulus_1.csv`), the response options offered (`option_1.csv`), and the raw inputs collected (`input_1.csv`). The trailing `_1` marks the attempt, so a repeated activity becomes `response_2.csv`, and so on.

Every table is tidy; every name follows the [naming conventions](/spec/conventions/naming.qmd); every column is defined in the [specification](/spec/index.qmd). You always know where things are and what they are called. (The full layout, including timeseries files, is in the [folder structure](/spec/conventions/folder-structure.qmd) specification.)

## Where BDM fits in the Behaverse ecosystem

BDM focuses on the dataset for a single study—everything you need to share all the data that study produced. But some parts of a dataset reach beyond it. For example, to make sense of a dataset you need its studyflow. Yet the studyflow also matters when running the study, processing its data, or building models of behavior. The boundaries between these concerns are genuinely blurred, which is why BDM is one piece of a broader set of tools that work together:

| Piece | What it is | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Data model** (this site) | The human-facing framework: conventions, concepts, guides, specification | [behaverse.org/data-model](https://behaverse.org/data-model) |
| **Schemas** | The machine-readable source of truth: JSON Schemas, field definitions, validators, changelogs | [behaverse.org/schemas](https://behaverse.org/schemas) · [GitHub](https://github.com/behaverse/schemas) |
| **Studyflow modeler** | Visual editor for study designs (studyflows) | [behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler](https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/app) |
| **Behaverse** | The broader project, including cognitive assessments, games, and more | [behaverse.org](https://behaverse.org) |

This site **defines** the prose conventions and renders summaries; the schemas repository **owns** every machine artifact (this site fetches them at build time, pinned by `schemas.lock`); the tools consume both. Additional projects are in progress (e.g., a modeling framework and a public catalog of BDM-formatted datasets); they will be listed here once ready (see the [roadmap](/roadmap.qmd)).

Within this site, the deep dives are one click away:

- The **rules**—naming, indexing, units, folder structure—live in the [Specification](/spec/index.qmd), alongside the field-by-field reference for every table.
- The **reasoning** behind the design lives here in Concepts: [design process](design-process.qmd) · [the nature of behavioral data](behavioral-data.qmd) · [metadata](metadata.qmd).
